implementation_notes: C# realises the monitor in the language and the BCL: the lock statement (Monitor.Enter/Exit in a try/finally, emitted by the compiler) is the monitor lock, and Monitor.Wait/Pulse/PulseAll are the monitor conditions, each locked object carrying a waiting queue and a ready queue. The compiler releases the lock on exceptions, which removes the classic release-on-every-path bug, and Monitor is reentrant with thread affinity. Since C# 13 the lock statement binds to System.Threading.Lock (EnterScope, a ref struct scope) for better performance, but Lock has no Wait/Pulse, so condition-based scheduling still uses Monitor on a separate object. In async code the whole structure is replaced by non-blocking serialisation, because await is forbidden inside a lock body.
pitfalls: Monitor.Wait/Pulse/PulseAll require the lock to be held and Pulse moves only one waiter to the ready queue: with a single per-object wait queue you normally need PulseAll plus a predicate loop.

Locking on this, a Type or an interned string lets foreign code share the lock; lock on a private dedicated object (or a System.Threading.Lock on .NET 9 and later) and never on a value type, because each call would box a fresh copy.
The lock statement cannot contain await, and blocking a thread-pool thread inside a monitor starves the pool; async code needs SemaphoreSlim or Channel based serialisation instead.

variants.name: SemaphoreSlim / Channel async serialisation
variants.implementation_notes: When the object is used from async code, blocking monitors are unusable - await cannot appear inside a lock body and would pin a pool thread anyway - so the monitor degenerates into an async serialiser: SemaphoreSlim(1,1).WaitAsync delimits the critical section and a second semaphore or a Channel carries the callers that must wait for the object's state to change. The serialisation guarantee is the same, but there are no monitor conditions, so predicates are re-evaluated after every await and capacity is signalled through the channel or semaphore rather than Wait/Pulse.
pitfalls: SemaphoreSlim must be a private field and every successful Wait must be paired with a Release in finally; a forgotten release wedges the object permanently and no monitor inspector will reveal it.
An async serialiser has no monitor condition: a predicate must be re-checked after every await, and spurious progress (cancelled waits, faulted tasks) must not leak permits.
